claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed nanoscale iron oxide/hydroxide surface film before exposure.
The native film is heterogeneous.
At room temperature, the native oxide/hydroxide film initially suppresses corrosion by acting as a barrier to electrolyte contact.
Elevated temperature in a chloride-rich harsh environment compromises the native film through cracking or phase transformation.
Thermal stress contributes to degradation of the passive film at elevated temperature.
Enhanced reaction kinetics at elevated temperature contribute to degradation of the passive film.
Film degradation exposes active iron sites.
Exposure of active iron sites accelerates localized corrosion.
Localized corrosion preferentially develops at microstructural heterogeneities such as inclusions.
Q235 steel exposed at approximately 70°C will show higher corrosion current density than a room-temperature reference under otherwise identical chloride, humidity, and duration conditions.
Q235 steel exposed at approximately 70°C will exhibit more pitting than the room-temperature reference.
Q235 steel exposed at approximately 70°C will exhibit more cracking or disruption of its surface film than the room-temperature reference.
At room temperature, untreated Q235 steel will corrode more slowly and more uniformly because its passive film remains intact.
The proposed mechanism applies only over chloride concentration and humidity ranges representative of harsh environments.
The proposed mechanism applies when temperature is high enough to compromise the surface film but not high enough to cause bulk phase transformations.
The proposed mechanism may not extend to steels with engineered surface treatments.
Microstructural variability between sample batches may alter the magnitude of the corrosion response.

Comparing matched Q235 samples at room temperature and approximately 70°C while holding chloride exposure, humidity, surface finish, and duration constant isolates temperature as the experimental variable.
EIS, polarization, SEM/EDS, and weight-loss measurements can jointly assess barrier behavior, corrosion kinetics, surface-film damage, pitting, and material loss.

Failure of the elevated-temperature samples to show a statistically significant increase in localized corrosion or film defects relative to the room-temperature control would falsify the proposed hypothesis.
